summary: SE-led 62m technical deep dive on long-context (>128k) strategies: hierarchical chunking, KV cache offload, batching tradeoffs, attention optimizations and on-prem considerations. Customer interested in POC to support 200k token retrieval use case with sub-second tail latency for short replies and tolerable increased latency for long reasoning pipelines.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-15 14:00 PT | Duration: ~62m | Attendees listed above.
[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, this is a technical deep dive focused on long context strategies, specifically targeting 128k+ prompts and beyond. Carlos will lead.
[00:22] Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE): Hi! cool, so Cerulean's ask we saw in the deck was roughly: ingest 200k tokens of multi-doc context, run a hierarchical retrieval + generation flow, and keep the short Q/A latency under ~300ms P50 when the reply is just a short answer. Is that still accurate?
[00:38] Dr. Lena Park (Cerulean): Yeah, that's the target. For many queries the model should only need the latest 4–8 chunks; we burn long context for deep reasoning jobs but want cheap fast answers for the rest.
[00:50] Jon Ortiz (Product): Also security: we need VPC, KMS, and the ability to keep KV cache inside our private subnet for the pilot.
[01:05] Carlos: Got it. I'll walk through two approaches: 1) hierarchical chunking with selective attention + compressed KV caching to NVMe, and 2) sliding-window full-attention with sparse attention kernels. We'll compare cost/latency tradeoffs and integration points for on-prem.
[01:28] Speaker 1: okay (laughs)
[01:32] Carlos: First, hierarchical chunking. The idea is we pre-chunk the corpus into variable-sized segments aligned around doc boundaries, then embed and index. At request time we do a two-stage retrieval: dense top-K (coarse) then re-rank with lightweight cross-encoder to pick ~8 chunks to stitch. This gives an effective context of 100–200k tokens but only pulls forward a small working set.
[01:55] Dr. Lena: The point of confusion for us was how the model still gets global coherence if you only forward small windows. How do you prevent hallucinations across chunk boundaries?
[02:10] Carlos: Good Q. We use hierarchical conditioning: global summary vectors per section and a multi-scale KV cache. The low-res summaries are fed as prefix tokens (or soft prompts), while the detailed KV entries for active chunks are kept in fast GPU memory or offloaded to NVMe with async prefetch. For long reasoning runs we also use re-entry points — re-encoding partial state into compact tokens every N tokens so attention doesn't need to reach back 200k tokens.
[02:37] Samir Patel (Cerulean): Sorry, NVMe offload — isn't that going to blow latency for the first token?
[02:45] Carlos: There's a trade. We prefetch predicted next-chunk KV asynchronously during generation; for short replies you rarely hit the cold NVMe. For heavy reasoning you might stall on fetching a chunk, but with good heuristics (lookahead + warm cache) stalls are kept to single-digit ms to a couple hundred ms depending on NVMe latency. We measured median cold-fetch ~40–80ms on our test infra, but can be higher on customer networks.
[03:12] Nina Park (Redwood SA): Also note we can keep a tiny bloom-filtered hot-KV in GPU DRAM — say top-3k keys — for sub-10ms lookups for the common prefixes.
[03:22] Jon: How much memory do you need on GPU for 128k tokens? With quant?
[03:29] Carlos: If you naively materialize full KV for 128k tokens and 32-bit, it's enormous — prohibitive. Typical production uses 16-bit or 8-bit KV entries and attention is handled with flash-attention kernels. With 8-bit (or GPTQ-style 4-bit for weights) the working memory per token drops. Example: on a 70B model with 128k context, full KV at 16-bit is ~xxx GB (demo numbers), we avoid that by chunking and only keeping active KVs. For a single active window of 8–12k tokens in GPU, plus hot-KV cache, you might need ~32–48GB of GPU memory depending on model architecture and kv format.
[04:10] Samir: The "xxx GB" above — I saw that in earlier slides — can you get us exact numbers? Our infra team needs hard numbers to size nodes.
[04:20] Maya: We'll attach the benchmark spreadsheet; Carlos will fill in model-specific numbers for your 70B and 13B candidates.
[04:29] Dr. Lena: On quantization — we run evals and saw some quality regressions with 4-bit GPTQ at long contexts. Does Redwood have guidance?
[04:40] Carlos: Short answer: yes, test on your evals. Longer: for retrieval-augmented pipelines, 4-bit weight quant (GPTQ) often works for generation if you keep KV and activations at 8/16-bit. Aggressive activation quant can hurt chain-of-thought. There's a config we recommend: GPTQ for weights + 8-bit activations + outlier handling for certain layers. We'll share config files.
[05:05] Speaker 2 (transcript mislabel): uh-huh
[05:09] Carlos: For attention optimizations we contrasted three kernel strategies: FlashAttention for contiguous attention, Block-sparse attention (our in-house grouping) for very long sequences, and grouped-query attention (GQA) which reduces compute by approximating cross-attention. Block-sparse gives best memory scaling but can increase complexity of kernel selection.
[05:33] Dr. Lena: Block-sparse sounds promising. Any pitfalls?
[05:36] Carlos: It requires model fine-tuning or at least structured pruning to be effective. Also kernel maturity differs across CUDA versions; FlashAttention is fairly robust on Ampere+ GPUs. Block-sparse needs careful benchmarking and may not be available on older drivers.
[05:53] Samir: We run a mixed cluster with A100 and H100. How do you recommend node configuration for on-prem POC?
[06:02] Carlos: For the POC, a small dedicated cluster of identical nodes is easiest: 4x H100 with 80GB, NVMe 4TB per node for KV offload, 512GB host RAM, and at least 100Gbps RDMA interconnect. That lets you test local NVMe offload and cross-node prefetch. If you must support A100 too, we'd pin different model variants per GPU type.
[06:28] Jon: What about orchestration? We prefer k8s with strict pod security policies.
[06:34] Nina: Redwood Private supports a control plane that can run in your VPC and the runtime can be deployed as k8s DaemonSets or as an air-gapped package. We can generate a minimum-privilege RBAC manifest for the POC.
[06:50] Dr. Lena: Any notes on licensing or model artifacts for our compliance team?
[06:55] Maya: We'll attach a short compliance pack: SOC2 outline, audit log format, KMS integration notes and the model license checklist.
[07:05] Carlos: Back to throughput/latency: we discussed a dual-path runtime — fastpath for short responses (limited local context + hot-KV + precomputed embeddings) and slowpath for deep reasoning (full hierarchical assembly + NVMe fetch). The runtime routes by SLO: if expected response tokens < 64 we go fastpath. If retrieval score variance high — go slowpath.
[07:33] Dr. Lena: How do you predict "expected response tokens"?
[07:35] Carlos: Heuristics + a tiny predictor model trained on your traffic. It looks at user intent signals and retrieval hit-rate. You can also explicitly call an endpoint with a 'fast:false' flag to force slowpath.
[07:48] Samir: Are there SDK changes needed? We already use your REST endpoint.
[07:52] Maya: For POC we'll recommend a shim layer that performs chunking + retrieval client-side and hits Redwood with the selected chunks. For advanced integration, our SDK supports automatic chunking and streaming KV prefetch hooks.
[08:06] Jon: Billing implications? This dual-path sounds complex.
[08:10] Maya: From billing perspective you pay per-token served plus a small NVMe storage/throughput fee for private deployments. We'll show estimated cost per query for different paths in the spreadsheet.
[08:22] Speaker 3 (Cerulean, unclear label): mm-hmm
[08:26] Carlos: A few gotchas: 1) tokenization drift — ensure the chunker uses same tokenizer as model otherwise offsets break; 2) attention recomputation tradeoffs — recomputation reduces memory but increases compute; 3) K-V cache eviction policies matter a lot for long tail queries.
[08:45] Dr. Lena: Could you expand on eviction? We have cold docs and hot docs, and want to prioritize hot docs.
[08:51] Carlos: Use LFU-style hot lists with TTL and retrieval-based touch signals. Also maintain a compact global summary that can be queried cheaply before deciding to pull full KVs.
[09:05] Nina: We also expose metrics for cache hit-rates, fetch latency, and per-route token counts in Redwood Console so you can tune policies.
[09:12] Samir: Any example numbers on P50/P95 latency for mixed workloads?
[09:16] Carlos: On our test cluster with H100s, fastpath P50 for short answers: ~45ms; P95 ~120ms. Slowpath median for long reasoning: ~350–900ms depending on number of NVMe fetches; worst-case few seconds if cold and multiple fetches occur. These are synthetic, your numbers will vary.
[09:40] Jon: For absolute SLA we need guarantees. Can Dedicated give SLOs?
[09:45] Maya: Yes, Redwood Dedicated includes SLA-backed latency targets per model tier and capacity reservation to reduce variance. For Private we offer optional SRE support.
[09:54] Dr. Lena: What about security boundary for KV cache on Private? Does it go to customer-managed KMS?
[09:59] Nina: Yes — keys are customer-managed. For air-gapped or on-prem installs the NVMe is on your nodes and logs can stay local; we provide a compliance manifest.
[10:10] Carlos: Quick note on attention ops: for really long sequences we sometimes do token-level compression (learned pooling) every 4k tokens so the attention window is hierarchical: exact attention to recent tokens, compressed attention to older sections. This keeps compute sublinear in sequence length.
[10:28] Dr. Lena: Interesting — any published benchmarks?
[10:30] Carlos: We'll share the whitepaper and our internal benchmarks. There's also an internal notebook that shows 2x throughput improvement on 200k workloads with hierarchical pooling vs naive windowing. Link will be in the sheet.
[10:42] Jon: On the infra side, will the POC require network changes? We have strict egress rules.
[10:47] Samir: yes, we limit outbound.
[10:49] Maya: For the POC we can take two approaches: 1) run full Private in your VPC with no egress, or 2) run a hybrid where the control plane is Redwood hosted but data plane is in your VPC with strict mTLS. We'll detail both.
[11:05] Carlos: One more performance trick: adaptive batching — the runtime grows the batch based on observed latency slack and predicted token counts. For long-context queries we often keep batch sizes small to keep tail latency down, but pack many short queries together. Continuous batching logic can reduce cost by 20–50% for high QPS.
[11:30] Dr. Lena: Is adaptive batching safe for memory-dense models?
[11:34] Carlos: We bound it by a memory budget per worker; if predicted batch would exceed memory we cap or split. Also dynamic quant profiles can be applied per-batch.
[11:45] Jon: How do you measure quality regressions when we change quant or chunking?
[11:50] Maya: Redwood Optimize ties prompts/evals to routes. We'll run A/B evaluation on your prompt suite and surface regressions in the Console. You can set automatic rollback policies.
[12:03] Carlos: Recap of proposed POC: 3–4 H100 nodes, NVMe offload enabled, hierarchical chunker preprocessor, hot-KV in GPU DRAM, GPTQ weights + 8-bit activations baseline, Redwood Private control plane in your VPC. We'll validate latency on shortpath and consistency on slowpath.
[12:20] Jon: Sounds good. Next steps again?
[12:22] Maya: See the next_steps items — we'll attach the sheet, whitepaper and draft POC topology. I'll book the POC checklist call for next week.
[12:31] Dr. Lena: Thanks everyone, excited to see the benchmark sheet.
[12:34] Carlos: Thanks all.
[12:35] Meeting end.

References and shared artifacts mentioned: bench spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/cerulean-128k.xlsx (placeholder), hierarchical chunking whitepaper (link to be shared), POC topology doc (will be attached).
